christoffel-symbols-64d17c83.conceptual_definition: Christoffel symbols are mathematical objects that arise in differential geometry and general relativity to describe the connection or "covariant derivative" in a curved manifold. They quantify how the basis vectors change from point to point in a given coordinate system, which is essential for defining parallel transport of vectors and determining the paths of shortest distance (geodesics) in curved spaces, such as spacetime. They are not tensors themselves but represent the components of the affine connection in a specific coordinate basis.
christoffel-symbols-64d17c83.intuitive_summary: Christoffel symbols essentially tell us how to "straighten out" or adjust our understanding of direction when moving in a curved space, allowing us to perform differentiation in a way that respects the underlying geometry.

qft-s-matrix-dyson-109f2c08.title: S-Matrix Perturbative Dyson Expansion
qft-s-matrix-dyson-109f2c08.interpretation: The Dyson expansion for the S-matrix, in its exponential form, is typically written as \( S = T \exp\left( -i/\hbar \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} H_I(t) dt \right) \). When expanded in a series, it becomes \( S = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-i/\hbar)^n}{n!} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dt_1 \dots \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dt_n T \left[ H_I(t_1) \dots H_I(t_n) \right] \). Here, \( S \) represents the S-matrix, which maps initial 'in' states to final 'out' states in a scattering process, providing the probability amplitudes for transitions. The operator \( T \) is the time-ordering operator, crucial for maintaining causality by arranging any product of time-dependent operators in chronological sequence from right to left. \( H_I(t) \) is the interaction Hamiltonian in the interaction picture, embodying the forces and couplings between particles that drive the scattering. Each term in the series corresponds to a specific order of perturbation theory: the \( n=0 \) term is the identity (no interaction), the \( n=1 \) term describes a single interaction, the \( n=2 \) term describes two interactions, and so forth, which can be visualized by Feynman diagrams. The integral extends over all time \( t \), reflecting the idea that particles are prepared and measured in asymptotically free states where interactions are negligible.
qft-s-matrix-dyson-109f2c08.symmetry_origin: The Dyson expansion itself is a consequence of solving the time-evolution operator for an interacting system in quantum mechanics using a perturbative approach, rather than directly stemming from a specific symmetry. It relies on the interaction picture formulation of quantum mechanics and the formal solution of the Schrödinger equation for time evolution. However, the specific form and content of the interaction Hamiltonian \( H_I(t) \) are profoundly dictated by underlying fundamental symmetries of nature, such as Lorentz invariance, gauge invariance, and other internal symmetries, which ensure the consistency and physical validity of the quantum field theory.
qft-s-matrix-dyson-109f2c08.limits_and_boundary: The validity of the Dyson expansion is primarily confined to the **perturbative regime**, where the interaction strength (or coupling constant, implicitly contained in \( H_I \)) is small. In this limit, higher-order terms in the expansion diminish rapidly, leading to convergence, and allowing for reliable approximations by truncating the series at a finite number of terms. Conversely, in the **strong coupling regime**, the series typically diverges or converges very slowly, rendering the perturbative approach unreliable and necessitating alternative non-perturbative methods. The integral limits from \( -\infty \) to \( +\infty \) imply that the system is considered in the adiabatic limit, where interactions are slowly turned on and off, allowing for the definition of asymptotic free particle states before and after scattering.

S.name: Scattering Matrix
S.description: The S-matrix (Scattering matrix) is an operator that describes the transformation of an initial quantum state of free particles into a final quantum state of free particles due to interactions. Its matrix elements give the probability amplitudes for various scattering processes.

T.name: Time-ordering Operator
T.description: The time-ordering operator arranges any product of time-dependent operators such that operators with later times appear to the left of operators with earlier times. It is crucial for maintaining causality in the Dyson expansion.

H_I(t).name: Interaction Hamiltonian
H_I(t).description: The interaction Hamiltonian in the interaction picture. It represents the part of the total Hamiltonian responsible for interactions between particles, which is treated as a perturbation. It typically depends on quantum fields evaluated at time \( t \).

t.name: Time
t.description: The independent time variable over which the interaction Hamiltonian is integrated, representing the duration and sequence of interactions.

i.name: Imaginary Unit
i.description: The mathematical imaginary unit, defined as the square root of -1. It is a fundamental component in quantum mechanics, arising from the complex nature of wave functions and amplitudes.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck Constant
\\hbar.description: The reduced Planck constant, \( h / (2\pi) \), a fundamental constant of quantum mechanics relating the energy of a photon to its frequency, or the angular momentum of a particle to its wave number. It is often set to 1 in natural units in quantum field theory for simplicity.

qft-s-matrix-dyson-109f2c08.conceptual_definition: The S-Matrix Perturbative Dyson Expansion is a fundamental series solution in quantum field theory that describes the time evolution of quantum states from an initial, non-interacting state to a final, non-interacting state due to an interacting Hamiltonian. It expresses the scattering matrix \( S \) as an infinite sum of terms, each representing a higher order of interaction, thereby providing a systematic method to calculate probability amplitudes for various scattering processes by treating the interaction as a perturbation to a free theory.
qft-s-matrix-dyson-109f2c08.intuitive_summary: This formula provides a way to calculate the total effect of quantum interactions on particles by summing up all possible sequences of individual interaction events, ensuring they occur in chronological order.

wimp-relic-density-25111797.title: WIMP Relic Density Relation
wimp-relic-density-25111797.interpretation:
The formula shows an inverse relationship between the relic abundance of WIMPs and their annihilation rate. eg{\( \Omega_{\chi} h^2 \)} is a dimensionless quantity that represents the fraction of the critical energy density of the universe contributed by WIMPs, with the Hubble parameter eg{\( h \)} squared ($h 
approx 0.7$, where $H_0 = 100 h$ km/s/Mpc) accounting for the expansion rate of the universe. The term eg{\( \langle \sigma v \rangle \)} is the thermally averaged product of the WIMP annihilation cross-section eg{\( \sigma \)} and their relative velocity eg{\( v \)}. A larger annihilation cross-section (meaning WIMPs are more likely to annihilate) or a higher relative velocity leads to a lower relic density, as more WIMPs would have annihilated in the early universe. Conversely, a small annihilation cross-section results in a larger relic density. The constant eg{\( 3 	imes 10^{-27} 	ext{ cm}^3	ext{ s}^{-1} \)} is derived from fundamental constants and cosmological parameters related to the freeze-out temperature and entropy density of the early universe.
wimp-relic-density-25111797.symmetry_origin: This relation originates from the thermal freeze-out mechanism in the early universe. As the universe expanded and cooled, WIMPs were in thermal equilibrium, constantly annihilating and being produced. When the rate of annihilation dropped below the expansion rate of the universe, WIMPs 'froze out' their number density. The relic density is determined by this freeze-out process, which is sensitive to the annihilation cross-section and the temperature at which freeze-out occurred.
wimp-relic-density-25111797.limits_and_boundary: As the thermally averaged annihilation cross-section eg{\( \langle \sigma v \rangle \)} approaches infinity, the WIMP relic density eg{\( \Omega_{\chi} h^2 \)} approaches zero, implying that if WIMPs annihilate very efficiently, they would not constitute a significant portion of the dark matter. Conversely, as eg{\( \langle \sigma v \rangle \)} approaches zero, the relic density would theoretically approach infinity, which is not physically realistic in a cosmological context and indicates that such a scenario would require additional physical processes (like asymmetric dark matter) or that WIMPs are not the correct dark matter candidate.
wimp-relic-density-25111797.conceptual_definition: This formula relates the cold dark matter density of the universe, represented by the WIMP relic density eg{\( \Omega_{\chi} h^2 \)}, to the thermally averaged annihilation cross-section and relative velocity of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs). It is a cornerstone of WIMP cosmology, providing a link between particle physics and astrophysical observations.
wimp-relic-density-25111797.intuitive_summary: The more efficiently WIMPs annihilate with each other, the fewer of them will be left over today as dark matter.
